# Performance And Scaling

**Example status — excerpt:** settings are tuning patterns, not portable
benchmarks or complete training jobs.

JSON2Vec performance is determined by the schema shape as much as by model
width. Fixed branch lengths, datatype capacities, data-loader behavior, and
prediction output can dominate before raw parameter count does.

Treat every throughput number as workload-specific. Record the schema, input
length distribution, hardware, precision, batch size, software version, and
output configuration next to the result.

## Measure The Whole Path

Separate four measurements:

| Measurement | Includes | Use it to diagnose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data preparation | Read, decode, preprocess, query, vocabulary/normalizer work | File format, workers, remote I/O, and Python transforms. |
| Encode + forward | Tensorization and model execution | Branch lengths, datatype capacity, model width/depth, device utilization. |
| Write/postprocess | CPU transfer, probability conversion, embeddings, top-k, reshaping | Oversized output contracts and Python serialization. |
| End-to-end service | Queue, dynamic batching, all stages above, JSON, network | User-visible latency and saturation. |

Lightning runs include JSON2Vec's `throughput/train`, `throughput/validate`,
`throughput/test`, or `throughput/predict` epoch metric. It estimates processed
observations from completed batches and configured model batch size. Use it for
comparisons under the same setup, then confirm important results with an
external end-to-end measurement.

Train, validation, and test throughput use Lightning's module-metric path.
Prediction has no Lightning result collection, so `throughput/predict` is kept
on the `ThroughputLogger` callback and sent directly to an attached logger; do
not expect it in `trainer.callback_metrics`.

## Control Repeated Context First

Every `Branch(length=...)` reserves a fixed number of positions. Short records
are padded; long records are truncated or rejected according to `overflow`.
For attention-enabled branches, work also grows with interactions among local
positions.

Before increasing a branch length:

1. measure the observed length distribution by split;
2. choose a percentile or business rule, not the maximum outlier;
3. select `overflow="head"` or `"tail"` from event meaning;
4. log truncation outside JSON2Vec if losing records matters operationally;
5. compare quality and throughput at two or three candidate lengths.

Nested branches multiply shape. A long child inside a long parent can create a
large padded tensor even when most observations are sparse. Window, filter, or
summarize irrelevant events in a preprocessor before expanding model capacity.

## Size Width And Depth

- `d_model` widens datatype embeddings, projections, attention, pooling, and
  decoders across the entire tree.
- `n_layers` adds sequential self-attention blocks to a branch.
- `n_linear` adds learned-query cross-attention pooling blocks; each block also
  contains a feed-forward network.
- `dropout` may improve generalization but does not reduce inference cost.

Increase width only after verifying the input contract and observing
underfitting. Increase depth only after a width comparison. Use
`sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())` for parameter size, but profile
representative activations because repeated context often controls memory.

## Compare Attention Modes

`mha`, `gqa`, and `mqa` share the same query-head count. GQA uses half as many
key/value heads (minimum one); MQA uses one. This reduces key/value projection
width, but local attention still considers the same positions.

`attention="none"` removes the branch's self-attention stack while retaining
learned query pooling. It is useful for short branches, low-cost baselines, or
testing whether cross-position interaction adds value.

Benchmark each mode on the intended PyTorch version and accelerator. Kernel
support and shape can matter more than theoretical parameter savings.

## Budget Datatype Capacity

### Category And Set

Category and Set content storage grows with `size × d_model`, and decoding or
scoring grows with `size`. A fixed-width projection elsewhere in a decoder does
not make a large vocabulary free.

- choose capacity from expected distinct training labels plus explicit
  headroom;
- monitor Category `vocabulary:size` by address;
- investigate capacity warnings rather than silently increasing every field;
- use `Entity` when only observation-local equality matters;
- keep high-cardinality join identifiers as metadata when they are not a model
  feature;
- avoid large `topk` output unless consumers use it.

### Text And Vector

Text cost depends on tokenizer/model choice and configured token length; it also
requires the `text` extra. Vector cost grows with source vector width and the
projection into `d_model`. Measure transfer and parsing as well as forward time
when vectors arrive from another service.

## Feed The Accelerator

For small in-memory work, `PolarsDataModule` removes file discovery and remote
I/O from the experiment. For larger jobs, tune `StreamingDataModule` with the
actual storage layout.

Important controls include:

- `num_workers`: parallel readers/preprocessors; too many can increase memory
  and contention;
- `persistent_workers`: avoids worker restart between epochs when workers are
  long-lived;
- `pin_memory`: useful for CUDA transfer, usually unnecessary for CPU-only work;
- observation and shuffle buffers: larger buffers improve mixing but consume
  memory;
- file/chunk/record sharding: choose from file sizes and worker/rank count;
- file format and row-group size: determine decode and remote-read granularity;
- `sample_rate`: useful for bounded experiments, not a substitute for a valid
  split.

Run a data-only or CPU baseline when the accelerator is idle. If increasing
batch size does not improve device utilization, the bottleneck may be query,
preprocessing, or I/O.

## Use Precision And Batch Size Deliberately

Configure numerical precision and accumulation on Lightning's `Trainer`. Start
with a batch that fits comfortably, then increase while watching memory,
throughput, and validation behavior.

Larger batches can improve device utilization but change the number of optimizer
updates per epoch. Preserve effective optimization conditions when comparing
throughput experiments—for example by controlling learning rate, accumulation,
and total update count.

Mixed precision can reduce activation memory on supported accelerators. Validate
numeric behavior for each datatype and loss rather than assuming identical
quality.

## Distributed Training

::: {.callout-warning title="Distributed support level"}
JSON2Vec provides Lightning-compatible distributed execution, streaming
sharding, vocabulary synchronization, and rank-partitioned output, and these
paths have focused tests. There is no cross-version distributed compatibility
guarantee or universal topology recipe. Pin the package, validate record
ownership and vocabulary state at the intended world size, and treat each
hardware/data layout as an integration you must benchmark.
:::

JSON2Vec registers callbacks that synchronize online vocabularies and place
late-created modules on the active device. Distributed runs still require a
consistent contract:

- every rank constructs the same schema and callback set;
- input shards do not overlap unless repetition is intentional;
- all ranks perform schema mutations in the same order between loops;
- vocabulary synchronization cost is included in the benchmark;
- global batch size and number of optimizer steps are recorded;
- validation/test aggregation is checked on more than one world size.

Scale only after one rank is input-efficient. More ranks amplify remote I/O,
worker count, vocabulary coordination, and output files.

## Optimize Prediction Output

Prediction can spend substantial time moving and serializing data:

- enable `embed=True` only at addresses consumers need;
- request only useful Category top-k values;
- use a postprocessor to remove internal or unused fields;
- use `Writer` for partitioned batch output rather than collecting a whole
  dataset in memory;
- set service `max_batch_size` and latency against the real request-size
  distribution;
- benchmark JSON backend and response schema validation separately.

An online latency target and an offline throughput target usually need different
batch sizes.

## Benchmark Record

Store at least this metadata with a result:

```yaml
json2vec_version: 0.4.11
device: "example: NVIDIA GPU model or CPU model"
precision: "32-true"
batch_size: 128
world_size: 1
records: 100000
branch_length_percentiles: {p50: 12, p95: 48, max_configured: 64}
d_model: 64
layers_by_branch: {record: 2, events: 1}
attention_by_branch: {record: mha, events: gqa}
output: {targets: [label], embeddings: [record], topk: 3}
measurement_boundary: "raw parquet read through parquet prediction write"
```

The values above are a reporting template, not a benchmark result.

## Failure Signals

| Signal | Diagnostic | Likely fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accelerator utilization is low | Time read/preprocess/encode separately from forward | Increase appropriate workers/buffers, simplify Python preprocessing, or fix remote I/O before widening the model. |
| Memory is high with mostly short histories | Compare observed lengths with configured branch shapes | Shorten/window branches or choose a justified overflow policy. |
| More ranks do not improve throughput | Check ownership, remote I/O, worker multiplication, and synchronization time | Correct sharding and remove the serial bottleneck before adding ranks. |
| Prediction is slower than training forward | Measure CPU conversion, top-k, embeddings, postprocessing, and writes | Narrow the output contract and use partitioned `Writer` output. |
| Callback throughput disagrees with load tests | Compare measurement boundaries and partial final batches | Publish both callback and end-to-end measurements with their exact boundaries. |
